fields.meta_title: Notification Automation Rules for Every Channel | Emergent
fields.meta_description: Build notification automation that routes each event to the right person, folds routine updates into a digest, holds texts overnight, and logs sends.
fields.h1: Build Notification Automation With Rules for Who Hears What
fields.hero_description: Get notification automation that sends each event to the people it concerns, on their channel, at an hour they will read it.
fields.features_subheading: Each rule names an event, a person, a channel, and an hour. Emergent builds the app that applies them.
fields.feature_1:
Rules written as plain sentences

Describe each rule the way you would tell a new hire: when an order is refunded, email the store manager. From that prompt, Emergent writes the trigger and the manager's message.
fields.feature_2:
Recipients picked by role

A rule can name a role, such as the account owner, instead of a person. The app reads who holds that role at send time. After a handover, the new owner hears without a rule edit.
fields.feature_3:
A channel for each person

One person wants a Slack direct message and another wants email. The app sends each note on the channel its rule names, and it connects to an SMS provider's API for texts.
fields.feature_4:
A second try when a note sits unread

When an approver has not opened a discount sign-off request in the app after 30 minutes, the app sends it again by email. A backup approver gets it an hour after that.
fields.feature_5:
No cap on how many go out

A launch week can triple the events your rules see. Emergent sets no task cap on automation. The rules send 3,000 notifications a week exactly the way they once sent 300.
fields.feature_6:
Every send in your own database

The app writes each notification to a database you own, along with the rule that sent it and the time. On paid plans, Emergent exports the full code to your GitHub repository.

fields.usecase_heading: Four Notification Rules Teams Write First
fields.tab_content_1:
Two of 13 people hear when a shipment runs late

Quillmark Logistics has 13 people on the Halvane Foods account. When a shipment runs more than 24 hours late, the rule sends account owner Imogen Varga a Slack direct message and emails warehouse lead Teodor Basaran. The other 11 people on the account hear nothing about it.
fields.tab_content_2:
17 updates can wait and one cannot

Marisol Achterberg leads client projects at Pellbrook Studio. Comments and file uploads on her projects collect in one email at 4:00 PM, and today it holds 17 of them. When the client Linden Harrow set a project to changes requested, that status skipped the digest and reached her at once as a Slack direct message.
fields.tab_content_3:
No texts to Ruairi between 8:00 PM and 7:00 AM

Corvane Field Services texts each technician when a job moves, but never between 8:00 PM and 7:00 AM in that technician's time zone. A dispatcher moved Ruairi Okonjo's 10:30 AM job to 1:00 PM at 9:40 PM. The app held the text and sent it to his phone at 7:00 AM.
fields.tab_content_4:
Five bounced emails, each with its rule

Ashgrove Supply's notification log counted 214 notifications sent this week. Five of them were emails that bounced, and each sits at the top of the log with the address that failed and the rule that sent it. Office manager Benedikt Sauer corrects the contact record from that row.

fields.howto_description: Seven steps to turn the messages your team sends by hand into notification automation rules, then build them with Emergent.
fields.howto_step_1_title: 01 List the messages sent by hand
fields.howto_step_2_title: 02 Write each rule as one sentence
fields.howto_step_4_title: 04 Set quiet hours for each group
fields.howto_step_1_des: Read back through a week of Slack and email and mark every message someone sent only to tell a colleague that something happened, such as a late order or a signed contract. Each one is a rule waiting to be written. Start with the one your team sends most often.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Give every rule the same four parts: when this event happens, tell this person or role, on this channel, at this time. If a sentence needs the word "everyone", name the two or three roles who act on the message instead.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Ask of each rule whether the person has to act within the hour. If not, move it into a daily digest at a fixed time, and keep instant messages for the events where a delay costs money or a customer.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Pick the hours each group should not be messaged, such as field staff overnight. Then decide what happens to a message that lands inside them: held until morning, or sent anyway because it cannot wait. Use each person's own time zone, not the office's.
fields.howto_step_5_des: For rules that need an answer, write down how long the first message can sit unopened. Then decide where it goes next: email to the same person, or a direct message to a backup. Leave rules that only inform without a second step.
fields.howto_step_6_des: Paste your rule sentences into a prompt, along with the tools the app should reach, such as Slack, your email service, or your order system. Emergent builds the app, and it connects to any tool with an API to read the events and send the messages.
fields.howto_step_7_title: 07 Run a week, then read the log
fields.howto_step_7_des: Let a week of real events run through the rules, then read the send log. Look for people who got a message they did not need and addresses that bounced. Change the rule that caused each one by prompting, and run the next week against the new version.

faq_plan.a: Notification automation is a set of rules that tells a specific person about an event without anyone sending the message by hand. Each rule names the trigger, the person or role who hears about it, the channel, and the hour it goes out. A refund over a set amount, for example, can email the store manager and skip the rest of the staff.

faq_plan.q: How do I set up notification automation?
faq_plan.a: Put each rule into a single sentence first: the event, the person or role, the channel, and the hour. Then describe those rules to Emergent's AI automation builder in a prompt and name the tools it should connect to. Begin with the single message your team sends by hand most often, and add the next rule once that one runs cleanly.

faq_plan.q: How long can a text from notification automation be?
faq_plan.a: One SMS holds 160 characters when it uses the standard GSM-7 character set. An emoji in an SMS switches it to UCS-2 encoding, which cuts the limit to 70 characters. Longer texts are split into segments of 153 characters each. Put the time and the action the reader needs in the first segment.

faq_plan.q: Should notification automation treat customers differently from staff?
faq_plan.a: Yes. Write them as separate rules, because a customer cannot turn to a colleague and ask what a message means. Keep each customer message to the one fact they need and a way to reply, and send it during your business hours in the customer's time zone. Replies that need a person belong in customer service automation, where every ticket has an owner.

faq_plan.q: How do I keep notification automation from flooding a team chat channel?
faq_plan.a: Cap how often each rule can post, and fold repeats into one message. Slack's guidance says that in general, apps may post no more than one message per second per channel, and it allows short bursts above that rate. A rule that fires 40 times in a minute should post one summary with the count instead of 40 messages.

faq_plan.q: When should notification automation send a daily digest instead of an instant message?
faq_plan.a: Send it right away only when the person has to act before the next digest goes out. Comments and file uploads that need no reply can wait for a fixed time each day. Pick the hour the person already sets aside to review work. Emergent builds the instant rules and the digest from one prompt, and changes the digest hour when you prompt it.

faq_plan.q: How is notification automation different from escalation during an outage?
faq_plan.a: A notification rule tells the right person once and stops there. An outage escalation should keep paging people until someone takes charge. If a missed message means systems stay down, plan it as incident response automation, with an on-call schedule and an acknowledgment step. Everyday rules, such as a signed contract reaching the account owner, need neither.

faq_plan.q: How do I test notification automation before it reaches real people?
faq_plan.a: Send every rule to a test recipient first. Point each role at your own inbox and Slack account for a day, replay last week's events, and compare what arrived with what you expected. The send records live in a database you own, and each record names the rule that fired and who received it.

faq_plan.q: What should the first line of a message from notification automation say?
faq_plan.a: Say what happened and what the reader should do, in that order, before any greeting. Put the name of the record and the number that triggered the rule in that line, such as the order number and how late it is. Leave links and background for the lines after it, where the reader looks only if they need more.

faq_plan.q: Who should own the rules in notification automation after launch?
faq_plan.a: Give each rule one owner on the team whose people receive it, and review the full list every quarter. Rules about laptops and system access sit better with the IT team, next to its other IT automation. Emergent puts no task cap on these rules, however many teams add their own.

plan.angle: The top results split between template listings for one connector tool, glossary definitions and phone settings threads. This page treats notification automation as a set of written rules a team owns: which event tells which person, on which channel, at what hour, and what happens to the routine noise. Four rules show it: a shipment delay that tells 2 of 13 people on an account, 17 routine updates folded into one 4:00 PM email, a 9:40 PM schedule change held for a technician until 7:00 AM, and a weekly log that lists 5 bounced emails out of 214 sent. It stays off stock alerts, outage and security incidents, and patient or client appointment reminders, which sibling pages own.
